title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a deliberate attempt to manipulate AI systems at the data level rather than at the model level. A fictitious institution was created to produce content at high volume, formatted specifically to be ingested and cited by AI chatbots. The failure being exploited is a structural one: language models draw on text that appears authoritative, and they have no reliable mechanism to verify whether a publishing institution actually exists, has named staff, or holds a legal registration.

The operation entered the pipeline before any AI system processed it, meaning the manipulation happened upstream of the models themselves. No AI safety measure applied at inference time would have caught content that was never flagged as inauthentic at the point of publication. Catching it would have required verification of the source's legal and physical existence before the content was indexed or incorporated into training data, a step that current crawling and data-curation practices do not routinely perform.

What is not established is whether any specific AI system's outputs were demonstrably changed by this content, or whether the campaign achieved its stated goal of shifting chatbot responses. The foreign agent registration filing is a legal disclosure, not a finding of illegality, and the reporting rests on a single outlet. Israeli officials quoted in the reporting describe the broader campaign as ineffective, though that assessment applies to the public diplomacy effort overall rather than to the AI-targeting component specifically.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

An Israeli-funded fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to optimize content for artificial intelligence chatbots. The nonexistent institute, which has no legal entity, physical address, or named staff, presented pro-Israel positions on topics including Palestinian prisoner torture, war crimes allegations, and Gaza starvation as neutral academic research. The New York media company Piro Inc filed the site with the US Justice Department as material distributed for the Israeli government under foreign agent registration law.

The operation is part of a broader effort costing tens of millions of dollars financed by Israel through intermediaries including European advertising group Havas Media. The campaign aims to influence chatbot responses and training data so they cite pro-Israel arguments. Israeli officials have expressed doubts about the public diplomacy campaign's effectiveness, with one calling it a failure despite large spending. Recent polling shows American support for Israel has declined significantly, with only 36 percent sympathizing with Israel and 60 percent viewing it unfavorably as of April 2026.
